stem: A client is experiencing dyspnea and respiratory distress. Which position is generally most helpful for improving chest expansion when no contraindication exists?

options.D: Flat prone position with the head turned to the side.

rationale: NCBI Nursing Fundamentals recommends raising the head of the bed to high-Fowler position for clients with hypoxia or dyspnea because upright positioning promotes chest expansion and diaphragmatic descent and can reduce the work of breathing. Tripod positioning is another useful upright option. B is therefore the best answer; lying flat or Trendelenburg can worsen diaphragmatic mechanics and dyspnea in many clients.
educational_objective: Use upright High-Fowler positioning, or another appropriate upright posture such as tripod, to support chest expansion and reduce dyspnea when clinically appropriate.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_document_title: Nursing Fundamentals, 2nd ed. — Part VIII: Oxygenation
source_locator: Table 8.2b Interventions to Manage Hypoxia — raise head of bed to high Fowler's; Applying the Nursing Process — high Fowler's or tripod position for dyspnea
source_claim_supported: High-Fowler/upright positioning promotes chest expansion and diaphragmatic descent and can reduce dyspnea/work of breathing.

source_original.stem: A client experiencing respiratory distress is most likely to benefit from which positioning?

options.A: Place the client flat in a supine position to reduce respiratory effort
options.B: Place the client upright in High-Fowler position to support lung expansion
options.C: Place the client prone with the head turned to limit chest wall movement
options.D: Place the client in Trendelenburg position to increase diaphragmatic pressure

source_original.rationale: High-Fowler's position (sitting the client upright, typically at 60-90 degrees) allows for maximal lung expansion by reducing pressure from abdominal organs on the diaphragm and optimizing chest wall movement, making it the preferred position for a client experiencing respiratory distress, unless otherwise contraindicated.
source_original.source_detail: High-Fowler/tripod positioning promotes chest expansion and reduces work of breathing; 2nd ed. 2024, accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Retained the correct upright-positioning intervention but removed unsupported angle precision and the absolute 'maximal/preferred' wording, added the no-contraindication qualifier and tripod alternative in the objective/rationale, and preserved easy difficulty.

audit_findings.source_authority: NCBI Bookshelf Nursing Fundamentals; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: 2024 second edition remains current and directly supports the basic nursing intervention.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Table 8.2b and the nursing-process section directly support high-Fowler/upright positioning for chest expansion and dyspnea relief; unsupported numerical angle and universal wording were removed.

distractor_audit.A: Supine positioning can worsen dyspnea and does not promote the same chest expansion.
distractor_audit.C: A flat prone position is not the routine positioning intervention described for dyspnea in this source.
distractor_audit.D: Trendelenburg increases abdominal pressure toward the diaphragm and is not the supported intervention.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Tripod is also useful but is not offered separately; B's upright High-Fowler position remains the single best listed choice.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are common body positions; the answer depends on respiratory mechanics and nursing positioning knowledge.
audit_findings.blueprint: Basic Care and Comfort is appropriate for positioning and comfort interventions.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read NCBI Table 8.2b and the nursing-process section, challenged whether tripod could create a second answer, ensured it was not offered separately, removed unsupported degree claims, and confirmed B remained uniquely best.
